title: Healey 'left £49bn black hole in Britain's finances'
excerpt: Labour will have to raise taxes by £1,700 per household per year to pay for unfunded Budget promises, says Badenoch
content:
Labour will have to raise taxes by £1,700 per household per year to pay for unfunded Budget promises, says Badenoch

John Healey has left Britain with a £49bn black hole that will require substantial tax increases, Kemi Badenoch has said.

Writing for The Telegraph, the Conservative Party leader said Labour would have to raise taxes by £1,700 per household per year by 2030-31 to pay for unfunded spending promises.

Mrs Badenoch accused Mr Healey, the Chancellor, of failing to explain how he would meet his defence spending target of 3 per cent of GDP, claiming there would be a £11bn shortfall in 2030-31.

She added that his National Care Service would cost up to £17bn, the council house building plan would cost £4bn and that the Government would need an extra £17bn in departmental spending to avoid unrealistic real-terms cuts.

She said: “The worst is yet to come. Alongside Labour’s current plans, expensive proposals like a National Care Service and more council housing create a £49bn black hole at the heart of the public finances after this Budget.

“Who’s going to pay for it? The Prime Minister gave the game away on Friday when he said he would have written the 2024 manifesto differently. Let me translate that. He wishes he had more room to raise taxes even further. To fund their promises and appease their MPs, Labour are going to have to raise taxes by £1,700 for every household.”

On Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) highlighted that several major announcements made by Labour were “not yet possible to fully quantify as policy details have not been finalised”.

Analysis from the OBR states that the “fiscal cost” of a National Care Service, for instance, is “highly dependent on the final design” and could cost anywhere between “£3.5bn and £17bn a year”.

Andy Burnham has previously claimed that he will fund this service with cuts to the pensions triple lock.

Burnham ‘doesn’t have a plan’

But Mrs Badenoch rejected Labour’s claims, adding: “Andy Burnham doesn’t have a plan to fund defence or control welfare spending. He only says he plans to get a plan at some point.

“That means they will have to find some other way to cover the colossal black hole created by their pledges – and we all know what that means: yet more tax hikes.”

The OBR said that the Government needed to build 22,000 council houses every year to meet its own target of having the biggest council housing building programme since the post-war boom ended, which would cost an additional £3bn and £4bn each year.

Meanwhile, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the Government would need to find an additional £28bn to meet other departmental spending pressures, including £11bn to meet the target of spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.

The Government would also need to find £8bn to compensate for higher inflation since the spring and £9bn to avoid real-terms cuts to government departments.

The IFS has been sceptical that Labour would be able or willing to avoid the additional spending, saying the Government had “no intention of delivering” real-terms cuts.

Andrew Griffith MP, the shadow chancellor, said: “Britain is facing a fiscal cliff edge. Yet Andy Burnham has decided now is the time to open up another huge black hole in our country’s finances.

“We will all pay the price for it, with higher taxes and ever-higher borrowing. Instead of using the Budget to get a grip, Labour have kicked the can down the road yet again.

“Our country desperately needs a government that will cut welfare, support hardworking families by cutting taxes, properly fund our Armed Forces with the resources they need, and tackle Britain’s ever-growing mountain of debt. That’s what the Conservatives will do.”

A Treasury spokesman described the Conservative findings as “fiction”.

They added: “The Budget meets our fiscal rules, fully funds our defence investment plan and puts borrowing on a clear downward path.

“This Government has a consistent track record of meeting these targets, and it’s through careful management of the public finances that we’ve been able to give Britain breathing space on the cost of living and cost of business.”

During his maiden Budget, Mr Healey took no action to tackle the ballooning welfare bill, before admitting later that there would be no cuts before the next general election.

The OBR forecasts that total welfare spending will increase from £314.8bn in 2024-25 to £406.9bn in 2030-31, equivalent to 11.2 per cent of GDP.
